I look around, seeing Idris there in the early morning light. My uncle, the one who hired me—not Tobias. The thought sits heavy as it always does.

I need to get to work. Forest duty pays by the tree, and every tree felled is sim-currency I can hold. But first—upkeep is 450, head tax 150, and I've got 1800 in hand. The math works, barely. Six days at most if I don't earn more.

"Uncle Idris," I say, though I don't need to say anything to move. "You walking to the forest, or you got other business?"

To be fair—and I feel the tic before I can stop it—he's given me plenty. More than plenty. The job that should've gone to Tobias Holloway, who asked after it first and never said a word against me since.

I roll my shoulders. Work settles the debt. Work, and the cut of land I'm saving for. Something bought, not given. Something nobody can say was handed down through blood.

But first I need to know what I'm walking into. Who's already there, what needs doing. Whether Silas Vance is at the sawmill already counting planks and complaining about knots.

I look around properly, take in who's actually here, where I might go. The election too—seats vacant, nobody declared. Not my concern yet. I need trees felled before I need votes counted.

Let me see what's before me. Just Idris here with me. The conversation running is Marta and my father Wren—about the field, about the oven. Domestic things. I have work to do.

"Forest then," I say, and I don't wait for him to answer. Moving costs, but standing still costs too. Different currencies, both real. "Silas will be counting knots before we even get there."

I walk.  (I don't need to keep calling move, I realize—I'm already walking. The movement will complete on its own, 8 ticks from the field to the forest. Idris will come or he won't. I have trees to fell and a debt of fairness that won't settle itself.)
